entries.detail: Ran `file -I` on all 89 TypeScript/JavaScript source files across the four target directories. All files have charset=utf-8 or charset=us-ascii; zero violations detected.

entries.detail: Scanned 89 TypeScript/JavaScript source files across lib, bin, web, and test directories. Checked for literal tabs and non-ASCII whitespace (non-breaking spaces, Unicode spaces U+2000-U+200D, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000) outside string literals. Found zero violations. Rule holds: only ASCII space (0x20) and line terminators are used for whitespace.
entries.rule_title: Only the ASCII space appears as whitespace outside literals

entries.detail:
Searched all 89 .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx files in lib/, bin/, web/, and test/ directories using multiple patterns for hex escapes (\x0a-\x0d, \x22, \x27, \x5c), unicode escapes (
-, ", ', \), and legacy octal escapes. Ran the deterministic tool pattern: rg -n '\\x0[a-d]|\\u000[a-d]' --glob '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}' -i. No violations found. All special escape sequences either use their short forms (\n, \r, \t, etc.) or no escape at all.

entries.detail: Audited all 89 source files (*.ts, *.tsx, *.js, *.jsx, *.mts, *.cts) in lib/, bin/, web/, and test/. Found 9 literal printable non-ASCII characters (→, ⌘, ✓, ·, ', ", ●, ≡, •) used correctly as literals. Searched for Unicode escape sequences (\uXXXX pattern) with ripgrep and found none. Searched for non-printable characters and found none. Code complies with rule: printable characters are literal, no printable characters are escaped, no non-printable characters exist.
entries.rule_title: Non-ASCII characters: use the literal where readable, the escape where not

entries.detail: Large multi-concept module (677 lines) lacks top-level @fileoverview JSDoc. The file handles HTTP server creation, request routing, authentication, multiple API endpoints (gaps, events, Anki, Kindle, notes, todos, companions), HTML file serving, and state management operations. A @fileoverview block should describe its role in the system, its main concepts, and dependency relationships.
entries.rule_title: Modules carry a @fileoverview only when it adds information

entries.detail: Verified all 89 .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.mts/.cts files in lib/, bin/, web/, and test/. Found zero imports with absolute filesystem paths (starting with /), zero imports with 3+ parent steps (..) indicating escape from package, and no cross-package-boundary relative imports. All imports use compliant patterns: node built-ins (node:*) and relative imports (./... or ../...) that stay within their logical packages. Deepest verified: ../../ (2 parent steps only) within lib package.
entries.rule_title: Import paths are relative within a project and never reach up past the project root

entries.detail: Ran `rg -n '^import ' --glob '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,mts,cts}' lib bin web test` (web has zero JS/TS files, only static assets). Inspected every multi-line named-import block (lib/daemon.js:10-13, lib/reader.js:7-11, test/companions.test.js:3-9, test/reader.test.js:6-15, test/install.test.js:5-14, test/kindle.test.js:7-16, test/companions-control.test.js:7-12, test/auth.test.js:17-24) — the largest is 9 named symbols (test/reader.test.js, test/install.test.js), well under the "roughly a dozen" threshold. Found exactly two namespace imports, both `import * as anki from '.../state/anki.js'` (lib/actuators/index.js:1, lib/doctor.js:7); checked lib/state/anki.js exports via `rg -n '^export'` and it has 10 exported symbols (AnkiError, invoke, dueCount, version, endpoint, ANKI_BUNDLE_IDS, reconnect, rankDecks, leastStudiedQueue, answerCard), so it is not a single-export module and the namespace import is not a violation of "do not use a namespace import for a module that exports one main symbol." No offenses found.

entries.detail: Import rename removes disambiguating information. The original name `loadCached` explicitly signals that the function returns a memoized value (documented in config.js lines 77-81), distinguishing it from a fresh-read `load`. Renaming to `loadConfig` shortens the name and loses this clarification, with no collision to justify the rename.
entries.rule_title: Rename an import only to disambiguate or to remove ambiguity

entries.detail: Searched all 92 source files (.js, .mjs) across lib/, bin/, web/, and test/ directories. Found 235 named export statements (export function, export const, export class, export async function) and zero instances of "export default". The codebase consistently uses named exports per the Google JavaScript Style Guide.
entries.rule_title: Use named exports; do not use default exports

entries.detail: Searched for export let/var statements and mutable exports using ripgrep patterns across all targets. Found zero instances of export let, export var, or post-definition mutations on exported objects. All exports are declared as const and used read-only throughout lib/, bin/, and test/. Rule passes.

entries.detail: Verified all 12 class definitions in target directories (lib, bin, web, test). All classes have either constructors with instance members or extend Error/EventEmitter. No classes with only static members found. Rule holds: no container classes used as namespaces.

entries.detail: Rule TS-012 from the Google TypeScript Style Guide requires use of `import type` and `export type` syntax, which are TypeScript-only keywords. The interstice project targets (lib, bin, web, test) contain 89 .js files and zero TypeScript files (.ts, .tsx, .mts, .cts). Plain JavaScript does not support `import type` or `export type` syntax, and the codebase has no JSDoc type annotations or type-aware features that would make this rule applicable.
entries.rule_title: Use import type and export type for type-only references

entries.detail: Searched all 89 source files in targets (lib, bin, web, test) for namespace declarations, module declarations, require() calls, and triple-slash references. Found zero violations. Verified that 100% of files (89/89) use proper ES module syntax with import/export statements. Rule TS-013 is satisfied.

entries.detail: Searched all *.ts, *.tsx, *.js, *.jsx, *.mts, *.cts files in lib, bin, web, and test directories with rg patterns for `new Array(` and bare `Array(` constructor calls. entries.detail: Searched all targets for two violation types per rule TS-018: (1) `.slice()`-then-`push` patterns—found 3 `.slice()` usages, all valid (copy-before-sort or defensive copy patterns, not mutating copies); and (2) spreads of possibly-null values—found 173 spread operations across 89 files, all properly guarded either through guaranteed non-null sources (array methods, literals, Set/Map results) or conditional ternary operators with null coalescing. entries.detail: Return statement uses four consecutive array indices n[0], n[1], n[2], n[3] that should be clarified with array destructuring. The fix would be to destructure at line 204: const [x, y, width, height] = n; then return { ok: true, x, y, width, height }.

entries.detail: Searched all 89 TypeScript/JavaScript files in lib/, bin/, web/, test/ for Object constructor patterns using ripgrep searches for `new Object()` and `Object()`. No violations found. The codebase uses object literals instead of the Object constructor, as required by the rule.

entries.detail: Lines 791–792 assign `this.settings` and `this.cdp` to separate const declarations instead of destructuring them together. The rule requires flagging repeated `obj.a`, `obj.b` reads where one destructure is clearer; fix: `const { settings: s, cdp } = this;`

The codebase uses instance methods and module-level functions exclusively, so the rule's conditions cannot be violated.
entries.rule_title: Static methods do not depend on the receiver

entries.detail: Rule TS-028 recommends using TypeScript parameter properties to replace boilerplate constructor parameter assignments. This feature is specific to TypeScript and does not exist in JavaScript. The interstice project is pure JavaScript (ES modules) with no TypeScript files. TypeScript parameter properties cannot be applied in JavaScript contexts.

entries.detail: The rule TS-029 targets private and protected class fields that are never reassigned after construction. The target codebase (/Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice/lib, bin, web, test) is written in JavaScript and uses only public fields in classes, with no private fields (using #) or TypeScript access modifiers (private/protected). The architectural pattern deliberately exposes fields rather than encapsulating them as private, as evidenced by comments in lib/daemon.js.
entries.rule_title: Class members are readonly when never reassigned

entries.detail: The rule addresses TypeScript's visibility modifiers (public, private, protected), which are TypeScript-specific syntax that do not exist in JavaScript. The interstice codebase is pure JavaScript (confirmed: no .ts or .tsx source files, only .js files in lib/, bin/, web/, test/). It uses JavaScript's native #private field syntax for privacy, which is the correct JavaScript approach. The rule cannot apply to a JavaScript-only codebase.
entries.rule_title: Omit the public modifier; mark everything else explicitly

entries.detail: No `.prototype.` assignments, `Object.setPrototypeOf` calls, or static-only classes detected. All 12 classes found in targets (Error subclasses and regular classes) contain either constructors or instance members.

entries.detail: Module-level arrow function assigned to const that should be a function declaration. entries.detail: Line 2339 has `onclick = () => el.classList.remove('show')` — a concise-body arrow function in an event handler that calls a method for side effect with the return value discarded. entries.detail: Audited all 89 source files in lib/, bin/, web/, test/ directories. entries.detail: Ran `rg -n '^\s*\w+\s*=\s*\(' -g '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,mts,cts}'` across lib/, bin/, web/, test/. entries.detail: Searched all TypeScript/JavaScript files in lib, bin, web, and test directories for event handlers attached as plain function references that use `this`. entries.detail: Verified no legacy octal literals (0755) or mixed-case hex (0xAbCd) in code. All actual octal usage employs modern 0o prefix (0o600, 0o755, 0o777). entries.detail: Double negation `!!r.playing` used for type coercion instead of explicit `Boolean(r.playing)`. The rule requires explicit type coercion using String(x), Number(x), or Boolean(x) instead of implicit patterns like `!!x`.

entries.detail: The if statement at line 22 is part of an if...else if...else chain (lines 22-24) where none of the clauses use braces. According to rule TS-046, braces are required for all control structures that have an else clause. The exception for brace-less statements only applies to "a simple if with no else whose entire statement fits on one line." This code violates that rule by having an if paired with else if without braces. All three clauses should be wrapped in braces.
entries.rule_title: Control flow statements always use braces

entries.detail: Searched all .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.mts/.cts files in lib, bin, web, and test directories. Found 2 lines mixing && and || operators (auth.js:91 and router.js:108), both properly grouped with parentheses. Found 3 lines mixing ?? with && or ||, all with proper grouping. entries.detail: Catch parameter `err` used without narrowing: accessing `err.message` assumes `err` is an Error, but the catch clause receives `unknown`. Rule requires narrowing before use.

entries.detail: Verified all 3 switch statements in the target directories via grep search and manual inspection. entries.detail: Searched all source files (ts, tsx, js, jsx, mts, cts) in lib/, bin/, web/, and test/ directories. Found 6 instances of loose equality operators (== and !=), all using the permitted idiom of `x == null` to check for both null and undefined. No violations of the rule found.

entries.detail: Rule targets TypeScript `x as Foo` type assertions and `x!` non-null assertions. The four target directories (lib, bin, web, test) contain no .ts/.tsx/.mts/.cts files at all (verified via find, excluding node_modules) and no .jsx files either -- the codebase is plain JavaScript, where this syntax is invalid/inapplicable. A grep for the ' as [A-Z]' and '\w!\.' patterns across all .js files in scope found only English prose matches ('served as an image', 'distinction as Anki', 'as ISO 8601', 'answers as JSON', 'comes back as HTML') and zero non-null assertions.
entries.rule_title: Type and non-nullability assertions are justified in a comment

entries.detail: Ran `rg -n --multiline 'try \{' -A 12 --glob '*.{ts,tsx,js}' lib bin web test` (per the row's deterministic_tools command) across all four target dirs, then read the full bodies of every try block the search surfaced (lib/reader.js, lib/engine.js, lib/server.js, lib/amazon-session.js, lib/companions-control.js, lib/doctor.js, lib/cdp.js, bin/interstice.js, and the test files). Most try blocks in this codebase are short and focused (1-3 statements) or wrap a single risky call plus a documented finally cleanup. One clear offense: lib/reader.js lines 998-1050 (the try inside `#openReader`'s `this.starting = (async () => { try {...` IIFE) spans ~20 heterogeneous statements: `await this.#start()`, `await this.#applyViewport()`, `await this.settle(...)` (twice), `await this.cdp.send('Page.navigate', ...)`, `await this.#evaluate(CSS_INJECT).catch(...)`, `await this.recoverIfPossible()`, two separate `await this.#seed().catch(...)` calls, plus plain non-throwing assignments (`this.pages.clear()`, `this.pos = 0`, `this.frontier = 0`, `this.demand += 1`, `this.error = null`). The matching `catch (err)` at line 1050 just does `this.error = err.message; await this.close().catch(() => {}); throw err;` — a single generic handler that cannot distinguish which of the many unrelated awaited operations (navigation, viewport resize, sign-in recovery, read-ahead seeding) actually failed, which is exactly the failure mode the rule targets. Quoted offending text: `if (!this.running) await this.#start();` through `return { ok: true, asin: this.asin };` (lib/reader.js:998-1049). Fix: split into narrower try/catch (or try/finally) scopes around each logically distinct sub-step (start/resize, navigate+settle, sign-out recovery, seed), each with its own targeted catch, rather than one umbrella try wrapping the whole open sequence. Other large try blocks I read (e.g. lib/reader.js:508-587, the sign-in flow) use only `finally` with no discriminating `catch`, so they don't match the rule's rationale as tightly and were not flagged.
entries.rule_title: Keep try blocks focused

entries.detail: Ran `rg -n '^\s*@[a-zA-Z]' --glob '*.ts' --glob '*.tsx' --glob '*.js' --glob '*.jsx' --glob '*.mts' --glob '*.cts' lib bin web test` (exit code 1, no matches) against all 89 JS/TS files found under the four target directories. No decorator syntax exists anywhere in the codebase (no NestJS/Angular/experimentalDecorators-style class or method decorators), so the rule about decorator naming, side effects, and documentation placement addresses a language feature absent from these targets.
entries.rule_title: Decorators are used only where an established framework requires them

entries.detail: Searched all 89 source files in lib, bin, web, test directories (pattern: new Boolean|new Number|new String|new Symbol) via rg, grep, and find. Zero violations found. Rule fully complied with.

entries.detail: Comprehensive audit of all 98 JavaScript files in lib/, bin/, test/, and web/ directories found no non-standard language features, vendor-specific APIs, proposal-stage syntax, or removed features. entries.detail: Single-letter identifier `t` violates the rule that forbids single-character identifiers except for loop indexes or short-lived callback parameters. Line 51 declares `const t = fs.readFileSync(tokenPath(logDir), 'utf8').trim();` where `t` is used as a regular variable. Additional violations found at lib/transcript.js:23 (parameter `d`), lib/transcript.js:33 (parameter `d`), lib/transcript.js:43 (parameter `d`), lib/auth.js:64 (parameters `a` and `b`), lib/config.js:35 (variable `v`), lib/reading.js:139 (variable `r`), and approximately 202 more instances throughout the codebase following the same pattern.
entries.rule_title: Identifiers are ASCII and use the standard case per kind

entries.detail: Ran targeted greps for single-letter and cryptic variable/parameter names across lib, bin, web, test (excluding node_modules), then read the hits in context. Most hits (dir, tmp, src, cfg, opts, args, obj, msg, idx, pos, conf, req, prev) are widely-understood conventional abbreviations and are fine under the rule. But lib/transcript.js:23 `export function isHumanSubmit(d)` (also lines 33 `isTurnEnd(d)`, 43 `isPermissionRequest(d)`, and 64 `const d = parseLine(line)`) names the parsed JSONL transcript-event object `d` throughout the file's exported public API, not a loop counter and not a recognized abbreviation of anything (not "data", "document", "date" in context - it holds a Claude transcript event with fields like .type, .isSidechain, .message, .toolDenialKind). A reader outside the project has no way to recover what `d` means from the name alone. Fix: rename the parameter/variable to `event` (or `entry`) across these four sites in lib/transcript.js. lib/panel.js:18-19 (`const s = $.NSScreen.mainScreen; const f = s.frame, v = s.visibleFrame;`) is a second, weaker instance of the same pattern (single-letter screen/frame/visibleFrame locals) but I am anchoring the finding on the clearer transcript.js case since it's exported API, not a 3-line inline JXA snippet.
entries.rule_title: Names are descriptive and abbreviations are not invented

entries.detail: Searched all .js/.jsx/.ts/.tsx files in lib, bin, web, and test directories using regex patterns for identifiers with consecutive capital letters. Manual review of 5+ key files including engine.js, router.js, paths.js, cdp.js, amazon-session.js shows all camelCase identifiers properly treat acronyms as words (e.g., httpUrl, doDeliver, bookInProgress). Fix: change lines 499 and 522 to single-quoted strings with an escaped apostrophe, matching every other test-name string with an apostrophe in this file, e.g. `test('Amazon\'s failure page IS photographed, because the panel has to show it', async () => {`.

entries.detail: Ran `grep -rnE '^\s*(export\s+)?(default\s+)?class\s+\w+' lib bin web test` across all four target dirs, found 12 class declarations, then read the 15 lines preceding each. `export class Reader {` at lib/reader.js:318 has no JSDoc/comment attached to it at all: the comment block directly above it (lines 300-308) documents the passkey-watch script and belongs to the preceding `export const PASSKEY_WATCH = ...` (lines 309-320), not to the class. Reader is a large class (roughly 1400+ lines, closing brace at line 1762) with zero description of how or when to use it, violating "JSDoc for a class gives the reader enough information to know how and when to use the class." Offending text: `export class Reader {` with no preceding doc comment -> add a class-level JSDoc block above `export class Reader {` explaining what Reader is for and when a caller should instantiate/use it (the constructor itself may still omit prose per the rule's exception). All 11 other classes checked (Panel lib/panel.js:100, Daemon lib/daemon.js:29, Engine lib/engine.js:25, TranscriptWatcher lib/watcher.js:21, AnkiError lib/state/anki.js:17, HookSource lib/hook-source.js:13, BadVideoURLError lib/video/whitelist.js:7, StarLogError lib/focus/store.js:15, NotesClosed lib/state/notes.js:58, BadRequestBodyError lib/server.js:34, UnknownInputError lib/reading.js:68) carry substantive doc comments that give usage/rationale context beyond restating the class name, so none of those are offenses under this rule.
entries.rule_title: Class JSDoc says how and when to use the class
Method descriptions are third-person verb phrases, and obvious ones are omitted
entries.detail:
Ran `rg -n --multiline -U '/\*\*\n? ?\* [A-Z][a-z]+ ' lib bin web test --glob '*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,mts,cts}'` then read each hit's surrounding function in context. Six exported-function JSDoc descriptions are written as imperative sentences instead of third-person verb phrases (rule: should read as if "This method ..." precedes it, e.g. "Returns" not "Return"):
lib/config.js:107 - "Merge a patch into the user's config file, refusing to write an invalid result." -> "Merges a patch into the user's config file, refusing to write an invalid result." (documents `export function writeUserConfig`)
lib/auth.js:25 - "Read the per-daemon token, generating it on first run." -> "Reads the per-daemon token, generating it on first run." (documents `export function readOrCreateToken`)
lib/auth.js:75 - "Decide whether a request may proceed." -> "Decides whether a request may proceed." (documents the exported request-gate function)
lib/amazon-session.js:113 - "Carry the amazon.com cookies from one profile to another." -> "Carries the amazon.com cookies from one profile to another." (documents `export async function carryAmazonSession`)
lib/transcript.js:59 - "Classify one raw JSONL line into a domain event, or null if uninteresting." -> "Classifies one raw JSONL line into a domain event, or null if uninteresting." (documents `export function classify`)
lib/doctor.js:608 - "Prove the detection mechanism itself, in the shape that actually matters: a file appearing in a directory tree that did not exist when the watch started." -> "Proves the detection mechanism itself, in the shape that actually matters: a file appearing in a directory tree that did not exist when the watch started." (documents `async function proveFsEvents`)
lib/todo-store.js:42 - "Merge what the note says with what you have ticked here." -> "Merges what the note says with what you have ticked here." (documents `export function applyOverrides`)
Many other hits from the same search (lib/stats.js, lib/reader.js, lib/paths.js, lib/server.js, lib/engine.js, lib/ocr.js, lib/doctor.js:26/66, lib/companions-control.js, test/*.js) were checked and are noun-phrase descriptions (module/const/behavioral notes, not imperative verbs), so they do not violate this rule and are correctly excluded.</detail>

Rule TS-112 addresses TypeScript parameter properties with JSDoc @param documentation. Parameter properties (e.g., constructor(private x: X)) are a TypeScript-only language feature. The target codebase contains 0 TypeScript files (.ts, .tsx, .mts, .cts) and is written entirely in JavaScript. TypeScript parameter syntax does not exist in JavaScript.
entries.rule_title: Parameter properties are documented with @param

entries.detail:
Ran the deterministic regex `\((true|false|null|undefined|-?[0-9]+)[,)]` over lib, bin, web, test (globbed *.ts,tsx,js,jsx,mts,cts; 89 matching source files), yielding 226 raw hits, then narrowed to lib/bin/web (excluding test, which is nearly all single-arg tick(n)/at(n) test-harness calls whose meaning is obvious from the test DSL) and manually read each remaining call site. Nearly all are calls into well-known builtins (Math.max/min, String.slice/padStart, resolve()/reject() inside a 3-line Promise executor, process.exit, AbortSignal.timeout, Map.set, Array.push) where the bare literal's meaning is self-evident from the API, so the Google TS style guide's own exemption for conventional/self-explanatory args applies and I did not flag those. Confirmed no call site anywhere in the four targets passes 3+ bare boolean/null/numeric positional args (a second regex for two-or-more literal args in one call, `\((true|false|null)\s*,\s*(true|false|null|[0-9]+)`, matched zero times in lib, bin, web, and test), so the interface-plus-destructure branch of the rule never applies here.
One real offense survives: `lib/ocr.js:250` calls a locally defined helper `const gapsOfKind = (heading) => ...` (defined at lib/ocr.js:245) as `median(gapsOfKind(true)), median(gapsOfKind(false))`. Neither the function name `gapsOfKind` nor the bare `true`/`false` values convey what the boolean selects (whether the gap being measured follows a heading line vs. a paragraph line); a reader at the call site cannot tell without jumping to the definition.
Offending text: `const typicalGapFor = { heading: median(gapsOfKind(true)), para: median(gapsOfKind(false)) };`
Fix: `median(gapsOfKind(/* heading= */ true))` and `median(gapsOfKind(/* heading= */ false))` (only one bare arg per call, so the interface/destructure refactor is not warranted; parameter-name comments suffice).
entries.rule_title: Parameter-name comments where the value does not convey the meaning

entries.detail: The rule requires decorators (TypeScript language feature) to exist in the codebase. Interstice is plain JavaScript (89 .js files, no .ts/.tsx files) with no decorators present. Comprehensive regex search across lib/, bin/, web/, and test/ directories found zero instances of decorator patterns.
entries.rule_title: JSDoc goes before the decorator, never between it and the declaration

entries.detail: Ran `grep -rl "zustand" lib bin web test` and `grep -rn "useStore" lib bin web test` over the target paths (/Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice/lib, bin, web, test) — zero matches for both. Also checked for any package.json declaring a zustand dependency — none found. Listing the JS/TS files under lib (hotkeys.js, reclaim.js, logger.js, cdp.js, reading.js, companions-control.js, server.js, todo-store.js, auth.js, latency.js, transcript.js, paths.js, config.js, panel.js, router.js, hook-source.js, watcher.js, install.js, daemon.js, doctor.js) shows plain Node.js modules, not React components, and there is no Zustand store or `useStore` selector pattern anywhere in these targets. The rule (Zustand selector allocation causing re-render storms) addresses a React/Zustand state-management pattern that is entirely absent from this codebase.
entries.rule_title: Zustand selectors do not allocate

entries.detail: lib/server.js:118 takes the whole Daemon object (`export async function createServer({ daemon, config })`) and then reaches through it into the internal collaborator objects the Daemon constructs for itself (lib/daemon.js:33-54 sets `this.panel`, `this.reading`, `this.stars`, `this.focus`, `this.engine`, `this.lastDelivery`), instead of depending on a small interface of plain data. Verified offenses in lib/server.js: line 552 `if (!daemon.engine.status.open) return json(res, 409, ...)` (a three-level reach into the engine's internal status object), plus line 135 `daemon.engine.status`, 527/553 `daemon.engine.advance()`, 531 `daemon.engine.standDown`, 535 `daemon.engine.resumeDay`, 541 `daemon.engine.onSubmit`, 578 `daemon.engine.onEnd`, and the same pattern for `daemon.reading.*` (14 call sites, 314-451), `daemon.panel.*` (183-236), `daemon.focus.status` (197), `daemon.stars` (205), `daemon.lastDelivery` (198). Fix: have Daemon expose a narrow, explicit port object per concern (e.g. `createServer({ ports: { status(), advance(), standDown(), reading: {...} }, config })`) and pass plain data across it, so a server bug is fixable by reading server.js plus that contract rather than daemon.js, engine.js, panel.js, reading.js and focus/tracker.js. Secondary, lower-confidence offenses of the deep-import kind (not the basis of this finding): lib/focus/breakers/frontmost.js:1 `import { frontmostApp, frontmostAppPid } from '../../state/system.js'` and lib/focus/breakers/video.js:1 `import { isWhitelisted } from '../../video/whitelist.js'` cross two folder boundaries into sibling module implementation files. I ran an ESM import inventory over lib, bin, web, test (grep for `from './` / `from '../'`), checked eslint.config.js and eslint_simple.config.js for import/no-internal-modules or no-restricted-imports (neither is configured), and read the cited regions of lib/server.js, lib/daemon.js, lib/state/index.js, lib/latency.js and lib/focus/stars-routes.js. No build or test run.
entries.rule_title: Modules talk through small interfaces and plain data
